title: Interior and Undertow
premise: Theo Galloway, a translator who has spent a decade burying Vessic—the dying language of the island community that raised her—recognizes her own voice on a radio broadcast: a lullaby she composed at fourteen and sang only once, to her dying mother. The recording leads her back to Saltmere Bay and to Marisol, the foster sister who kept singing it, and to a community deciding whether their language can survive in exile. As Theo translates the last living speaker's testimony, she must finally speak Vessic aloud—at her mother's grave, before the tide takes the old village seawall—to grieve properly and claim the found family she abandoned.
about_author: Zephyrine Eastwick is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two coastal towns and two grammars of silence. Her fiction explores how communities keep what empires cannot translate.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In her London flat, Theo translates a novel while reaching for a Vessic word for 'grief' and finding only English waiting. She catalogs her losses in a notebook. Emotional beat: quiet erosion—the reader sees a woman fluent everywhere except inside herself.

chapters.title: A Song With No Name
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A late-night radio program plays an unlabeled folk song; Theo freezes—it is hers, written at fourteen, sung once to her dying mother, never recorded. The host says it came from a listener in Saltmere Bay. Beat: vertigo; the buried past knocking.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Theo's POV. Ten years earlier: her mother's deathbed, the single singing, and Theo's vow of silence after relatives called the language 'shameful island noise.' Beat: origin of the wound.

chapters.title: Return Ticket
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. She buys a ticket to Saltmere Bay without telling her partner Daniel, telling herself it's research. On the train she practices one sentence of Vessic and can't finish it. Beat: fear disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Village That Moved Uphill
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Saltmere Bay has half-relocated inland as the sea eats the old shore; the lower town is condemned but inhabited by holdouts. She hears Vessic in a shop and flees. Beat: home as a place she no longer has permission to enter.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The foster sister who stayed recognizes Theo at the harbor café but doesn't reveal herself yet; instead she leaves a copy of the song's cassette on Theo's table. Beat: a door opened without forcing.

chapters.title: Cassette
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In her rented room she plays the tape: her own adolescent voice, then Marisol's harmonies added over years of solitary singing. She weeps for the first time since the funeral. Beat: grief arriving on schedule, ten years late.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Marisol introduces Theo to Aunt Ivet, ninety-one, the last fluent speaker, who refuses to greet Theo in English. Theo answers in broken Vessic—her first spoken words in a decade. Beat: shame cracking into tentative belonging.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Ivet's POV. Ivet agrees to record her life story—but only if Theo translates it, because 'a language lives when someone carries it across water.' Theo accepts, terrified. Beat: vocation becoming obligation.

chapters.title: Daniel Calls
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, intercut with phone calls. Daniel gives an ultimatum: come home or end it. Theo realizes she's been translating him too—softening herself into palatable English. Beat: the price of survival made personal.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confesses she recorded Theo's song from outside the hospital window all those years ago; her decade of singing was penance and love. Theo's fury and relief collide. Beat: the found family's first honest wound.

chapters.title: The Condemned Houses
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The council schedules final demolition of the lower town, including Theo's childhood house. Holdouts plan a farewell festival in Vessic. Theo is asked to translate the program—and declines, panicking. Beat: rising stakes; retreat.

chapters.title: Words That Don't Come Back
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo attempts translation and finds her vocabulary gone; she rages at herself, nearly burns the notebook. Ivet tells her: 'You didn't lose it. You hid it. Hiding is also keeping.' Beat: reframing loss as survival.

chapters.title: The Mother's Grave
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo visits the clifftop cemetery, finds her mother's stone weathered, and speaks a full Vessic sentence aloud to the sea—halting, wrong, real. Beat: the almost-saying ends.

chapters.title: Festival Preparations
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating short sections. The village cooks, rehearses, argues about whether the festival is mourning or resurrection. Theo sews banners with words she's relearning. Beat: communal warmth; belonging offered.

chapters.title: Ivet Falters
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Ivet suffers a small stroke; her speech scatters into Vessic no doctor understands. Only Theo can interpret at her bedside. Beat: urgency crystallizes—time is running out.

chapters.title: Translation Under Pressure
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Through long nights, Theo renders Ivet's scattered testimony into coherent English, discovering Ivet's hidden history: she once chose English for her children, believing she was saving them. Beat: mirror held up—Theo sees her own choice reflected backward.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Demolition crews arrive early; the festival may be cancelled. Theo stands before the diggers and—in full, unbroken Vessic—demands they wait until sundown tomorrow. They do. Beat: climax approach; the voice fully claimed.

chapters.title: The Festival of the Lower Town
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The whole village gathers among condemned houses; songs, food, Ivet wheeled down in a chair. Theo sings her mother's lullaby publicly, Marisol harmonizing. Beat: catharsis; grief sung out loud together.

chapters.title: Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At dawn Theo performs the traditional Vessic farewell rite at the seawall—naming the dead, releasing them—then calls Daniel and ends the relationship gently, choosing not to translate herself away again. Beat: resolution of the central debt.

chapters.title: Carrying It Across
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, months later. Ivet has died peacefully; Theo publishes the bilingual testimony and stays in Saltmere Bay, teaching Vessic to children in the new school. Beat: survival redefined—not preservation, but passage.

chapters.title: Interior
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, final page. On the radio, a child from Saltmere Bay sings the lullaby, now credited. Theo listens in her kitchen, answering the chorus under her breath, every word intact. Beat: quiet joy; the language lives because someone finally said it.
